strengths: The paper addresses a practically significant and well-formulated problem: transferring robustness from a foundation/teacher model to a compact student when the training dataset suffers from unknown covariate shift and completely missing subgroups.

The proposed method, ConfiG, is conceptually clear and well-motivated. Formulating the generation objective to simultaneously maximize teacher confidence (preserving class semantics) and minimize student confidence (counteracting spurious reliance) is intuitive and effective.

The empirical results are strong and compelling. On CelebA and SpuCo Birds, ConfiG delivers substantial gains in worst-group accuracy over competitive diffusion-based augmentation baselines (e.g., achieving 66.1% worst-group accuracy on CelebA, nearly closing the gap to the CLIP teacher at 66.7%).

The paper provides an extensive set of ablations and analyses, including evaluations across diverse student architectures (ViT-T, TinyViT, ResNet-18), different dataset sizes, cost-vs-quality trade-offs against baseline expansion factors, and compatibility with bias mitigation methods like TAB.
weaknesses: High computational cost: As discussed in Section A.7, ConfiG requires decoding through the VAE and backpropagating through the iterative diffusion process at every optimization step (taking ~11.4 seconds per image vs. ~3.3s for ActGen). While the cost-vs-quality analysis in Table 8 partly justifies this overhead, the multi-step generation pipeline remains computationally heavy.

Pipeline complexity: The framework requires a multi-stage process—training an auxiliary biased student on real data, running gradient-based latent optimization through diffusion for data augmentation, and finally retraining a new student on the combined dataset.

Dependence on teacher availability and robustness: The framework critically depends on having a teacher that is already robust to the specific covariate shift. On SpuCo Birds, the off-the-shelf zero-shot CLIP teacher failed (achieving only 40.2% worst-group accuracy), requiring the authors to train an artificial teacher on fully balanced data. While honest and properly discussed in the limitations, it highlights a practical constraint when off-the-shelf foundation models cannot disentangle task semantics.

Theoretical contribution is largely confirmatory: Proposition 1 relies on strong assumptions (such as uniform $\ell_\infty$ bounds on teacher calibration/accuracy across train, test, and generated support) that essentially formalize the intuition that generating high-loss student samples where the teacher is accurate reduces empirical risk discrepancy.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated formulation: The core idea of using the disagreement between a robust teacher and a biased student to guide diffusion generation directly targets learned shortcuts without requiring explicit group annotations or prior knowledge of the spurious features.

Strong empirical gains on group robustness: ConfiG achieves impressive gains on worst-group accuracy across benchmarks (e.g., boosting CelebA worst-group accuracy from 38.9% to 66.1%, nearly matching the CLIP teacher at 66.7%, and achieving 62.7% vs. 52.7% for ActGen on SpuCo Birds).

Sound theoretical and empirical justification: The paper provides theoretical grounding in Appendix A.1 showing how confidence-guided augmentations reduce the generalization gap under covariate shift, supported by informative analytical checks (e.g., Table 2 evaluating student loss/accuracy on generated images).

Extensive experimental analysis: The authors provide thorough ablations including the quantity vs. quality tradeoff (Table 8), compatibility with existing bias mitigation frameworks (TAB), different student backbones (TinyViT, ResNet-18), and augmentations combined with CutMix/MixUp.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on teacher robustness: The framework fundamentally hinges on having an oracle-like teacher that does not share the student's susceptibility to the spurious feature. As the authors acknowledge, when zero-shot CLIP failed on SpuCo Birds (40.2% worst-group accuracy), an explicitly fine-tuned teacher on balanced data had to be substituted, which may not always be available in practical unknown shift scenarios.

Computational overhead: Optimizing Equation 7 in the latent space requires full decoding at each optimization step, resulting in a runtime of 11.4 s/image on an NVIDIA V100 (compared to 3.3 s for ActGen and 2.1 s for unguided generation). Although ablated in Appendix A.5/A.7, this cost limits scalability to large-scale datasets.

Benchmark scale: The primary group-shift experiments are conducted on small subsampled subsets (500 training images for CelebA and SpuCo Birds). Evaluating on standard full-scale distribution shift benchmarks (e.g., WILDS datasets such as Waterbirds or Camelyon17) would provide a stronger test of scalability and robustness.

strengths: Compelling problem formulation: Addressing unknown covariate shift and group absence in knowledge distillation without requiring demographic/group annotations is an important practical challenge.

Technically sound and intuitive methodology: Guiding diffusion latents by maximizing teacher confidence while minimizing student confidence elegantly identifies and perturbs spurious features without degrading causal features.

Theoretical foundation: The authors support the intuition with a formal derivation (Proposition 1 and Lemma 1 in Appendix A.1) bounding the reduction of the generalization gap under explicit assumptions.

Strong empirical gains: ConfiG achieves substantial improvements in worst-group accuracy over existing diffusion-based data augmentation baselines (e.g., +12.1% on CelebA and +10.0% on SpuCo Birds over ActGen), along with consistent improvements on Spurious ImageNet.

Extensive experimental analysis: The paper provides meaningful ablations including different student architectures (TinyViT, ResNet-18, ViT-T), synergy with model-centric debiasing (TAB), and thorough cost-vs-quality analysis comparing multiple baseline expansion factors.
weaknesses: Strong dependence on teacher robustness: The method assumes that the teacher does not share the student's reliance on spurious features. In SpuCo Birds, off-the-shelf zero-shot models failed and required fine-tuning the teacher on balanced data, which partially compromises the realistic setting where balanced data is unavailable.

High computational overhead: Optimizing through diffusion decoding requires multiple backward passes per sample (11.4 s/image on V100 vs. 3.3 s for ActGen and 2.1 s for SD), making data synthesis noticeably slow for larger datasets.

Multi-stage distillation overhead: The workflow necessitates training an auxiliary biased student, performing iterative latent optimization via null-text inversion, and finally retraining the target student, which adds complexity compared to standard KD pipelines.

Evaluation is focused on relatively small-scale subsets: The group shift datasets are restricted to small subsamples (500 training images), and while realistic for data-scarce scenarios, testing on larger-scale benchmark setups would further strengthen the claims.

strengths: Clear, intuitive, and well-motivated concept: leveraging teacher-student disagreement via guided diffusion generation to discover and populate underrepresented/absent data slices under covariate shift without explicit group annotations.

Strong empirical improvements across multiple benchmarks (CelebA-HQ, SpuCo Birds, BAR, ImageNet-100), exhibiting significant gains particularly on worst-group accuracy (WGA) and group mean accuracy (GMA) compared to existing diffusion-based data augmentation techniques.
Rigorous and fair baseline comparison: the evaluation accounts for differences in computational cost across methods by matching generation FLOPs via baseline sample multipliers.

Extensive analysis and ablation studies, covering the individual components (inter-class mixing vs. latent optimization), stronger classical augmentations, compatibility with single-step fast diffusion models (Hyper-SD), weaker teacher models, and model-centric debiasing methods (LfF, uLA).
weaknesses: High computational overhead during data generation: the latent optimization requires iterative backpropagation through both classifier models and diffusion denoising/inversion steps, which can be expensive to scale to larger datasets or high image resolutions despite matching FLOPs with baseline multipliers.

Strong dependence on teacher robustness: the effectiveness of ConfiG hinges on the assumption that the teacher model is already robust and accurate across the missing groups. When the teacher is less robust or exhibits biases itself (as explored in Tab. 7 and on the BAR dataset), the performance gains diminish.

Complex multi-stage generation pipeline involving auxiliary student distillation, null-text inversion, prompt-to-prompt editing, latent optimization with segmentation/foreground regularization (HQ-SAM), and subsequent student distillation.

strengths: Compelling and intuitive core idea: Leveraging the disagreement between a robust teacher and a biased auxiliary student to guide diffusion-based augmentations towards unseen or shortcut-dominated regions without requiring explicit group annotations.

Rigorous experimental design with fair computational budget matching: The authors explicitly match the generation computational cost (in FLOPs) across six competitive diffusion-based augmentation baselines (GIF, DistDiff, DA-Fusion, Diff-Mix, Diff-II, ActGen) and report means and standard deviations across multiple runs.

Strong and consistent empirical improvements in worst-group accuracy (WGA), group-mean accuracy (GMA), and SpuScore across several group-shift benchmarks (CelebA-HQ, SpuCo Birds, BAR) and ImageNet-100.

Extensive analysis and ablation studies: The paper provides theoretical justification, ablates each component (inter-class mixing vs. latent optimization), tests compatibility with stronger non-synthetic augmentations, investigates weaker teachers and different model architectures (ConvNeXt), and demonstrates compatibility with model-centric debiasing methods (ERM, LfF, uLA) and single-step diffusion models.
weaknesses: Multi-stage generation pipeline complexity: ConfiG requires training an initial auxiliary student, performing null-text inversion, running per-image latent optimization guided by both teacher and student forward/backward passes, and then training the final student model. This adds significant operational overhead compared to standard KD or direct generative pipelines.

Dependence on teacher robustness: The method fundamentally relies on the assumption that the teacher model is well-calibrated and free from the target spurious correlations. As shown in the weaker-teacher ablations (Table 7 and Table 22), when the teacher itself possesses blind spots, the performance of the distilled student degrades noticeably.

Less pronounced gains in non-shift or less structured settings: In the natural, balanced few-shot setting without covariate shift (Table 24, Oxford Pets), ConfiG underperforms or only matches existing baselines like Diff-Mix, indicating that the targeted disagreement objective is specialized for distribution shift scenarios.

strengths: Clear problem formulation addressing a practical and challenging setup: knowledge distillation under unknown covariate shift and group imbalance without access to group annotations.

The proposed confidence-guided optimization objective (ConfiG) is intuitive and well-targeted: simultaneously enforcing high teacher confidence (preserving class semantics) and low student confidence (targeting student shortcuts) effectively generates hard counter-examples to spurious features.

Commendable baseline comparisons with fair computational matching: unlike many data augmentation papers that simply compare 1-to-1 synthetic sample generation, the authors explicitly estimate generation FLOPs and give baselines corresponding multi-sample generation budgets (e.g., up to 28x or 36x multipliers).

Substantial and consistent performance improvements across multiple spurious correlation and group-shift benchmarks (CelebA-HQ, SpuCo Birds, BAR, ImageNet-100), especially on worst-group accuracy (WGA) and spurious score (SpuScore).

Extensive ablations and sensitivity analyses, including the decoupling of inter-class mixing vs. latent optimization, compatibility with stronger standard augmentations (MixUp, CutMix, AutoAugment), single-step diffusion models (Hyper-SD), and varying teacher/student capacities.
weaknesses: High computational complexity and pipeline overhead: generating augmentations requires backpropagation through the diffusion model decoder and classifiers over multiple optimization steps, as well as pre-training an auxiliary student first to capture the dataset biases.

The theoretical justification in Appendix A relies on strong and largely circular assumptions (e.g., assuming in Eq. 14 that the augmented distribution Q is strictly more challenging for the student than the teacher by a margin, and that the teacher is well-bounded on the support of Q), which serves more as a formal restatement of the desired premise than a predictive bound.

Potential vulnerability to generative artifacts and semantic drift: optimizing latent codes to minimize student confidence can drive generations toward out-of-distribution or adversarial regions (as shown in the failure cases in Appendix Fig. 10), which necessitates ad-hoc regularizers (e.g., HQ-SAM foreground distance constraints) and rejection heuristics.

Evaluation is limited to classification tasks with relatively small numbers of classes (up to ImageNet-100). The scalability and efficiency of randomly selecting target classes and running inversion-based editing on datasets with thousands of fine-grained categories remain unclear.
